holidays.name: Polar Bear Plunge Day
holidays.description: Brave (or slightly unhinged) souls race into freezing cold lakes, rivers, and oceans on the first morning of the year, usually wearing costumes and enormous grins to hide the chattering teeth.
holidays.origin: Cold-water New Year dips date back generations. The Coney Island Polar Bear Club in Brooklyn began its New Year's Day swim in 1903, and many cities around the world have since copied the tradition.
holidays.funFact: Some plunges draw thousands of participants. Canada's Vancouver Polar Bear Swim has been held since 1920 and is one of the oldest such events in the world.

holidays.name: Bloody Mary Day
holidays.description: An unofficial holiday dedicated to the classic tomato-juice cocktail, nicknamed the ultimate hangover cure after a night of New Year's Eve revelry. Garnishes get wildly extravagant, from celery stalks to entire sliders on a skewer.
holidays.origin: The drink is often credited to bartender Fernand Petiot, who is said to have created it in the 1920s at Harry's New York Bar in Paris. It became linked with New Year's Day as the morning-after remedy of choice.
holidays.funFact: Fernand Petiot later brought the drink to New York's St. Regis Hotel, where it was renamed the Red Snapper because the original name was considered too crude.

holidays.name: Global Family Day
holidays.description: A day dedicated to peace and sharing, built around the idea that the whole world is one big family. Participants are encouraged to start the year by saying 'One day in peace' to someone.
holidays.origin: Launched in 1997 by the One Day in Peace organization, inspired by the idea of a single day of global ceasefire and goodwill. It is observed as a peace-minded alternative way to kick off the new year.
holidays.funFact: The core idea is that if people can make peace for one day, they can try to do it again the next. The day is also tied to a push for a worldwide ceasefire.

holidays.name: Hangover Day
holidays.description: The unofficial day of recovery, when much of the world is nursing regret, headaches, and a deep need for greasy food and darkened rooms. Pajamas, toast, and sports-drink toasts are the unofficial uniform.
holidays.origin: It grew out of New Year's Eve party culture, where the morning after naturally became its own unofficial holiday. People started recognizing it informally, and it has become a running joke on social media every January 1.
holidays.funFact: Many cultures have their own regional morning-after cures, such as Poland's pickle juice, Mexico's menudo soup, and Romania's tripe soup.

holidays.name: Z Day
holidays.description: A tongue-in-cheek day for the last letter of the alphabet, celebrating all things Z, from zebras and zippers to zombies and a good snooze. Naturally, it comes at the start of a new year, when plenty of people are catching some extra Zs.
holidays.origin: This is a light-hearted unofficial observance, largely spread by calendar-of-weird-holidays sites and social media. It plays on the fact that people often sleep in on New Year's Day.
holidays.funFact: The letter Z is the least-used letter in the English alphabet by some counts, and Americans say 'zee' while most of the English-speaking world says 'zed'.
